core_classification.analysis: Will’s embedded “I love you” unequivocally presents his love for Dorothea as a true, continuing emotional state. It does not undertake a relational commitment: indeed, he insists that poverty makes their belonging to each other impossible. Although the scene and delivery are intensely emotional, the words remain an avowal rather than an independently evidenced reflex-like discharge.
core_classification.ambiguity: The clause is embedded in a concessive hypothetical (“Even if you loved me as well as I love you”), but Will’s own love is treated as the factual baseline rather than as hypothetical.

utterance_status.description: Will directly speaks the love avowal to Dorothea, embedding it within the concessive conditional comparison “Even if you loved me as well as I love you.”

contextual_interpretation: Will confesses his love while arguing that mutual love would still be insufficient to overcome his poverty and their apparent inability to marry. His failure to maintain his intended silence and the passionate, storm-framed encounter establish emotional intensity, but not a separate expressive/reflexive force. The utterance avows love while his surrounding speech rejects hope of a viable union rather than committing him to one.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “Even if you loved me as well as I love you”
evidence.supports: The comparative construction treats Will’s love as an affirmed factual baseline, strongly supporting T.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “It is impossible for us ever to belong to each other.”
evidence.supports: Will explicitly frames a shared relationship as impossible, weighing against performative commitment or undertaking force.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “I meant to go away into silence, but I have not been able to do what I meant.”
evidence.supports: The confession breaks through Will’s intended silence and is emotionally pressured, but this alone does not establish reflex-like E force.

evidence.quotation_or_description: The narration says Will spoke “passionately,” while the pair clasp hands, kiss tremblingly, and discuss separation and possible marriage.
evidence.supports: The scene confirms intense and sincere-seeming romantic avowal, while passion and bodily emotion remain contextual delivery evidence rather than independent E evidence.

evidence.quotation_or_description: The occurrence is in George Eliot’s Middlemarch, Chapter LXXXIII, and is identified as an affirmative present-tense explicit love expression.
evidence.supports: Confirms the textual location and grammatical form of the classified occurrence.

ontology_assessment.diagnosis: T naturally captures the avowal’s core force. The surrounding passion, frustrated courtship, and renunciation of hope require contextual explanation but reveal no important core-force dimension missing from T/P/E.
